Sunday, May 26, 1935.
Dear Bebs:
I am on the way from Chungking to Hankow after a most strenuous
party in Szechuen during which it was quite impossible to write and even
If I had written the letter would just have waited to come along with us
on this plane.
You will remember that we arried in Chungking last
Monday and that I did not know what we would do after we got there.
However we learned that Chiang Kai-shek was planning to leave Yunnan-fu
right away for Kweiyang and would arrive Chungking on Thursday so we
stayed in Chungking for an appointment there on Friday.
Dr. Jones and
Chevalier went over to Chengtu.
Mr, Carroll, Gov. Fores and 1 remained
at Chungking•
We were booked solid for breakfast, tittin and dinner with
meetings in between.
Nothing of any special interest, mostly long con-
Perences on possible industrial and railroad projects in Szechuen Province.
Friday afternoon Rogers and Remer joined us and I was very much pleased
Remer especially was willing to fly again with CNAC after Broiles
dumped him into the whangpoo.
They were both good sports in every way
and I thanked them as sincerely and whole heartedly as I could.
Rogers
broke a small bone in his right foot and Remer broke one of those short
ribs that caused me so much pain when I broke my arm.
Well we had made an appointment with the "Generalissimo" for
fore o'clock Friday afternoon.
Gov, Forbes, Rogers and I were

way that runs to Chengtu. We elimbed a long flight of stone stairs
Leading from the drive up to the house - soldiers all around - soldiers
whose uniforms fit them and who wore shoes instead of "sneakers".
passed they came to a real snappy salute which we tried to acknowledge
with the easy nonchalance of those acoustomed to such deference.
At the
door of a typically foreign house such as you would find belonging to the
President of the First National Bank of Anywhere, Kansas, we were ushered
into a formal parlor and presently General Chiang and Mrs. Chiang came in.
The General wore a uniform without any decoration
or insignia of rank -
just as plain as K. I. Nieh's or old deacon Swann's of the First Congrega-

He is 48 years old but

37, typically Chinese.

eventually we shall get some action but I have memorized Kipling's
poem:
"It is not good for the Christian White
To hustle the Aryan Brown
The Christian riles
And the Aryan smiles
And he weareth the Christian down
And the end of the fight
Is a tombstone white
With the name of the late deceased
This Epitaph drear
A fool lies here
Who tried to hustle the Bast."
We planned to leave Chungking on Saturday but Chiang Kai-shek
invited the whole party for dinner Saturday night and requested Gov.
Forbes and Mr. Carroll to make an inspection trip in Marshall Chang
Hsueh-liang's Boeing from Chungking to Changsha
and Nanchang,
on to Shanghai.
They are leaving Tuesday.
Dr. Jones and 1 are trying
to catch the Taft out of Hongkong on Tuesday and we therefore decided
to leave on schedule Saturday in order to give us one day's leeway
for bad weather and also a day at Shanghai.
However Saturday the
weather turned very bad with low or no visability and we remained in
Chungking which proved to be very fortunate.
Saturday morning I had
a long talk with Mr. Donald, now Chief advisor to Chiang Kai-shek.
Donald is an Australian who years ago organized a magazine call ed
Far Bast Review.
It became very successful.
Finally Mr. Donald's
partner sold out the controlling interest to the Japs and the magazine
became a medium of Japanese propaganda.
Donald gave up his interest
and became an adviser for Chang wwwkektang Tso-lin, the old Manchurian
War Lord.
He has subsequently acted in the same capacity for the
Young Marshall Chang Hsueh-liang and Just now is serving with Chiang
Kai-shek.
He is an old friend of Mr. Carroll and the latter agreed
that if I would go to Manila for the American Mission, which he as
Vice-Chairman and Gov. Forbes as Chairman both urgently requested,
that he Carroll would have a long confidential talk with Donald.
Accordingly when we did not fly I sat in with Carroll and Donald for
a three hour talk in which we discussed the whole commercial aviation
program.
Donald understands and promised to set Chiang and Madam
Chiang, which is fully as important, straight on the whole subjeat.
complete memoranda with him and he told me that both Chiang
and Madam Chiang were favorably impressed with my verbal presentation.
All of us Americans are in trouble because of unwillingness to fly
bombs into Kweiyang•
The Italians (please tell Col. Drysdale) did
so and got away without any serious trouble.
Harry Smith who has
flown Chiang Kai-shek's Ford all over China and who even carried bombs
(under protest) has been dismissed so rumor has it;
Reed Knight and
Tommy Taylor, Hangehow School instructors, have both been dismissed
for the same
They all agreed to carry the bombs if the
detonators were removed and sent in another airplane as for instance
a Chinese Army bomber.
The detonators are in themselves highly danger-
our, the bombs not so bad - but the two together in any slight accident
or rough landing might be just too bad.
We are involved because the
Minister of Communications was asked
to instruct CNAC to fly the bombs
and the Minister of Communications without contacting the company wired
back that Pilot Nelson would do so.
Of course when Bond and I refused
to order or even ask Nelson to fly bombs the M. of C. Lost face and
that is of course most unfortunate.
Later we had a talk with M.Y.Tang
and as a result Bond and I notified the M. of C. that we would both
fly to Chungking for a talk with Nelson.
If then Nelson was willing
to take a leave of absence from NAC and go to work for the Chinese
Army on terms of pay satisfactory to him we would give him every
possible assistance in the way of mechanies service, radio, weather
data, ete.
This was declined - but at least we got
credit for making

the offer.
Saturday night Gov. Forbes, Mr. Cerroll, Rogers,
Remer,
Dr. Jones, Chevalier and I all went
to dinner with the Chiang Kai-sheks.
The dinner was foreign style with knives and forks - very simple and
addition to us were Mr. Donald, Dr. Liu and General Chiang's
confidential secretary.
Gov. Forbes sat on Madam Chiang's right
Rogers on her left.
Carroll sat on the General's right and I sat on
his left.
So you see we aviation men received preferred consideration
at least. Your boy friend Chevalier much to his apparent discomfort
sat between the non-English speaking Secretary and
the many-language-
knowing no-language-speaking taciturn Dr. Jones.
"Chevy" couldn't
have been more effectively muzzled and I suspect someone must have
tipped off Madam Chiang to arrange the seating that way.
always insists on all members of the Mission wearing that ridiculous
red rayon badge to every function and got furious when I refused to
wear it on my dinner coat to the Chiang's party.
Obviously the only
reason for ever wearing it is for purposes of identification and
certainly it was quite out of place at & private dinner.
I urged them
all not to go looking like a delegation of small town Rotarians but
I was the only one without a badge and believe I caught a faint smile
of approval from Madam Chiang.
After dinner something very funny happened - Gov. Forbes asked
General Chiang for an autographed pieture, whereupon the General asked
me if I wanted one too and quite naturally I said that I would like
one very much. A secretary brought a lot of pictures and the General
autographed one for each member of the party "to Mr.
from Chiang
Kai-shek" using the Chinese characters on our respective cards.
card was last in the stack and he only had six pictures so he sent
upstairs for another portrait which was much better and considerably
larger - inseribed it to me and said through Madam Chiang as inter-
preter "Last and best."
Of course I'm glad to have it but don't know
what on earth to do with it and would rather have had a smaller one.
I wired you this moming early advising you of my plans to
go to Manila and will be looking forward to hearing whether or not
you are all 0K.
Got your first letter and one From Frances at Hankow.
Called up the MeCleskey/s and invited myself for supper - gave them
your best - also saw the Josslyns at a cooktail party given us by
Schillings - Standard 011 No. 1 at Hankow.
Now approaching Shanghai.
Probably won't write again until we start for Hongkong tomorrow.
Forgot to tell you that Leighton Rogers cabled New York immediately
after the accident to put the brakes on the publication of any stories
about his injury.
His office cabled back "Congratulations you made
the front page of every newspaper in America stop as a publicity stunt
it was a wow exelamation point recommend more conservative methods."
Professor Remer who is a statistician and who was making his second
flight said that there had been four accidents on CNAC lines and he
had been in 25% of them also that 50% of his flights had ended in a
crash - also that he had been in 50% of the accidents in which no one
was killed (Geo Rummill & Broiles).
They have both been good sports
and that has helped me over a situation which you can well imagine
has been a most distressing one from many angles.
Lots of love and I'11 be looking forward to seeing you when
I come back.
Herold
